explanations.explanation: Right on the money, friend. The LORD tells Moses, Israel's leader, to say to the people: “…you may bring as your offering an animal from the herd or the flock.” (Leviticus 1:2) A bull comes from the herd, and a few verses later the flock turns out to mean sheep or goats (Leviticus 1:10). Two choices, both named, and nobody had to guess.

Good guess for hauling the load, but those two aren't on the LORD's list. He says the animal comes “…from the herd or the flock.” (Leviticus 1:2) The herd is cattle and the flock is sheep or goats (Leviticus 1:10). I bet the camel would've loved being picked, though.

Deer and gazelles never make the list, friend. The LORD says the animal comes “…from the herd or the flock.” (Leviticus 1:2) Sheep or goats make up the flock (Leviticus 1:10), and a burnt offering of birds can be a turtledove or a young pigeon (Leviticus 1:14). Chasing a gazelle across the hills sounds like a very long way to go for a drop-off.

That's the one. The LORD says, “If his offering is a burnt offering from the herd, he is to present an unblemished male.” (Leviticus 1:3) Two words do the work there: male and unblemished. God was specific, so the man brings what God asked for.

Close to a real rule, but not this one. For a burnt offering from the herd, the text says “…an unblemished male.” (Leviticus 1:3) It doesn't say firstborn, and it doesn't say female. Females do show up later in the peace offering (Leviticus 3:1), so hang onto that for when we get there.

The size of the animal never comes up, friend. The text asks for “…an unblemished male.” (Leviticus 1:3) Later in the chapter it calls it a young bull (Leviticus 1:5). So the LORD names the kind to bring, and a full-grown ox isn't part of it.

explanations.answer: The entrance to the Tent of Meeting
explanations.explanation: That's the spot. The man brings it “…to the entrance to the Tent of Meeting for its acceptance before the LORD.” (Leviticus 1:3) That's the same tent the LORD spoke from when He called to Moses, Israel's leader. The place is named, so there's no wandering around looking for it.

explanations.answer: The bank of the Jordan River
explanations.explanation: The Jordan never gets mentioned in this passage, friend. The man brings the offering “…to the entrance to the Tent of Meeting…” (Leviticus 1:3) That's where it gets accepted before the LORD. I'd hate to see the traffic if everybody dropped off at the river instead.

Nice try, but no mountain climbing is needed here. The LORD is speaking from the Tent of Meeting (Leviticus 1:1), and that's where the man brings his offering: “…to the entrance to the Tent of Meeting…” (Leviticus 1:3) Mount Sinai isn't named in these instructions. The place that is named is the entrance of that tent.

explanations.answer: So it can make atonement for him
explanations.explanation: You've got it. The text says, “He is to lay his hand on the head of the burnt offering, so it can be accepted on his behalf to make atonement for him.” (Leviticus 1:4) The hand on the head is part of how the offering is accepted for him. The man isn't just a bystander at his own offering.

explanations.answer: So the priest knows it is his
explanations.explanation: I can see how you'd land there, but the text gives a different reason. The hand goes on the head “…so it can be accepted on his behalf to make atonement for him.” (Leviticus 1:4) Nothing there is about the priest keeping track. I think a hand on the head says plenty about whose offering it is, but the text names atonement.

explanations.answer: So it stays calm at the altar
explanations.explanation: That would be a nice bonus, friend, but the text never says it. The reason it gives is “…so it can be accepted on his behalf to make atonement for him.” (Leviticus 1:4) The hand on the head is about atonement and acceptance. Keeping the animal calm isn't in the verse.

Yes, friend. The text says, “…Aaron’s sons the priests are to present the blood and splatter it on all sides of the altar at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.” (Leviticus 1:5) The man has his own jobs, like slaughtering the young bull before the LORD. Presenting and splattering the blood is the priests' work.

The elders aren't mentioned in this part, friend. The job goes to “…Aaron’s sons the priests…” (Leviticus 1:5) The man has plenty to do himself: he slaughters the young bull (Leviticus 1:5), then skins it and cuts it into pieces (Leviticus 1:6). But the blood is handled by the priests.

Moses is the one hearing all of this from the LORD (Leviticus 1:1), but the blood isn't his job. Neither is it Joshua's, and he's Moses's assistant (Exodus 24:13). The text gives it to “…Aaron’s sons the priests…” (Leviticus 1:5) Two big names, and neither one is on the blood crew.

That's right. The text says, “The entrails and legs must be washed with water, and the priest shall burn all of it on the altar…” (Leviticus 1:9) The word is must, so the washing comes first. Same instruction shows up again for the flock (Leviticus 1:13).

Not this time, friend. The text says the opposite: “The entrails and legs must be washed with water…” (Leviticus 1:9) So the washing happens, and it comes before the burning. The priest then burns all of it on the altar.

All of it goes up, friend. First the animal is skinned and cut into pieces (Leviticus 1:6), and the entrails and legs are washed. Then the text says, “…the priest shall burn all of it on the altar as a burnt offering…” (Leviticus 1:9) Everything laid on that altar gets burned, with nothing held back.

Only the fat would leave an awful lot behind, friend. For the burnt offering, the text says the priest burns “…all of it…” (Leviticus 1:9) The head and the fat were arranged on the wood with the pieces (Leviticus 1:8). Fat has its own spotlight later, with the peace offering, and that list includes the kidneys and the lobe of the liver too (Leviticus 3:3-4).

The head does go on the altar, friend, but it's not the whole story. The text says the priest burns “…all of it…” (Leviticus 1:9) The head and the fat were arranged atop the burning wood along with the pieces (Leviticus 1:8). So the head is in there, along with everything else.

Sheep is right. The text says, “If, however, one’s offering is a burnt offering from the flock—from the sheep or goats—he is to present an unblemished male.” (Leviticus 1:10) So the flock means sheep or goats. The rule about an unblemished male stays the same.
Goats are right, friend. The flock in this verse means “…the sheep or goats…” (Leviticus 1:10) Either one works for a burnt offering. And the same rule applies: an unblemished male.

Cattle is where the first option came from, so I get it. But the verse says the herd is where the bull comes from (Leviticus 1:3-5). The flock is “…the sheep or goats…” (Leviticus 1:10) So cattle belong in the other pen.

Camels? Big personality, but the verse doesn't invite them. The flock is “…the sheep or goats…” (Leviticus 1:10) That's the guest list, and the camel is standing outside the door with a very confident look. Sheep and goats are your two.
Donkeys don't make the list here, friend. The flock is spelled out as “…the sheep or goats…” (Leviticus 1:10) Nothing else gets added. I bet the donkey would've been very confident about it too.

North it is. The text says, “He shall slaughter it on the north side of the altar before the LORD…” (Leviticus 1:11) Then the priests splatter the blood against the altar on all sides. The side of the altar is named right there in the verse.
South isn't it, friend. The verse says, “He shall slaughter it on the north side of the altar before the LORD…” (Leviticus 1:11) Same verse, and the direction is right there. Compass check: north.

West doesn't show up in this verse. The text gives the direction plainly: “He shall slaughter it on the north side of the altar before the LORD…” (Leviticus 1:11) The priests then splatter the blood against the altar on all sides. The slaughter is on the north side.

explanations.answer: A turtledove or a young pigeon
explanations.explanation: You nailed it. The text says, “If, instead, one’s offering to the LORD is a burnt offering of birds, he is to present a turtledove or a young pigeon.” (Leviticus 1:14) So the burnt offering isn't only about bulls and sheep. Birds are on the menu too, and I love that the verse is so specific about which ones.

explanations.answer: A raven or a young eagle
explanations.explanation: Big birds, big ideas, but neither is on the list. The verse says, “…he is to present a turtledove or a young pigeon.” (Leviticus 1:14) Those are the two named. A raven and an eagle aren't offered anywhere in this passage.

explanations.answer: A sparrow or a young quail
explanations.explanation: Close in size, friend, but not the right birds. The text says, “…he is to present a turtledove or a young pigeon.” (Leviticus 1:14) That's the whole list for this offering. Sparrows and quail aren't named.

The text says the opposite, friend. The bird is torn open by its wings “…without dividing the bird completely.” (Leviticus 1:17) So it isn't split in two. Then the priest burns it on the altar atop the burning wood.

That's right. The text says, “He shall tear it open by its wings, without dividing the bird completely.” (Leviticus 1:17) The head has already been twisted off (Leviticus 1:15) and the crop removed (Leviticus 1:16), so this bird isn't whole anymore. But it isn't split in two either. Then the priest burns it on the altar atop the burning wood.

Oil goes on the flour, friend. The text says, “When anyone brings a grain offering to the LORD, his offering must consist of fine flour. He is to pour olive oil on it…” (Leviticus 2:1) It's olive oil, poured on top. That's the first of the two things.

Frankincense is the second one. The verse says the person is to “…put frankincense on it…” (Leviticus 2:1). The priest later burns the handful together with all the frankincense (Leviticus 2:2). So it goes on with the oil.

Honey sounds right to a cookie guy, but it's not on this list. The verse names olive oil and frankincense (Leviticus 2:1). Honey actually gets a no later: “…you are not to burn any leaven or honey as a food offering to the LORD.” (Leviticus 2:11) So keep it in the cookie jar.

Myrrh isn't in this verse, friend. The grain offering gets olive oil poured on the fine flour and frankincense put on it (Leviticus 2:1). Nothing else is named for this step. Myrrh doesn't come up in this whole passage.

Wine doesn't show up in this passage's grain offering. The verse says the fine flour gets olive oil poured on it, and frankincense put on it (Leviticus 2:1). That's the whole list. A nice thought, but the LORD named the two.

explanations.answer: It belongs to Aaron and his sons
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The priest burns a handful as the memorial portion, and the rest belongs to Aaron and his sons (Leviticus 2:3). They're the priests (Leviticus 1:5). The text calls it “…a most holy part of the food offerings to the LORD.” I would have guessed the man takes it home, so I'm glad the text is clearer than my guessing.

explanations.answer: It goes back to the man who brought it
explanations.explanation: Nice try, friend, but the man doesn't take it home. The text says the remainder “…shall belong to Aaron and his sons…” (Leviticus 2:3), and those are the priests (Leviticus 1:5). I bet it feels odd to hand over a batch you worked on and not carry any back. But that's how this one goes.

explanations.answer: It gets burned the next morning
explanations.explanation: Nothing in this passage says it gets burned the next morning, friend. What goes up in smoke is the handful, as the memorial portion (Leviticus 2:2). The remainder “…shall belong to Aaron and his sons…” (Leviticus 2:3), and they're the priests (Leviticus 1:5). The text calls it “…a most holy part of the food offerings to the LORD.”

That's the recipe. Baked in an oven, it's fine flour with unleavened cakes mixed with oil or wafers coated with oil (Leviticus 2:4). On a griddle it's fine flour mixed with oil (Leviticus 2:5), and in a pan it's “…fine flour with oil.” (Leviticus 2:7) Different cookware, same two things.

Barley and water don't show up here, friend. Every version uses fine flour with oil (Leviticus 2:4-7). What changes is how it's made: baked cakes and wafers in the oven, bread on a griddle, or a pan version that says plainly, “…fine flour with oil.” (Leviticus 2:7) Different cookware, but the same two ingredients.

The flour is right, but honey is out. Every version uses oil (Leviticus 2:4-7). In fact, the LORD says, “…you are not to burn any leaven or honey as a food offering to the LORD.” (Leviticus 2:11) So fine flour with oil is the answer.

You got it. For the griddle offering, the text says, “Crumble it and pour oil on it; it is a grain offering.” (Leviticus 2:6) It's unleavened bread made of fine flour mixed with oil (Leviticus 2:5). So crumbling and pouring both happen.

It's true, friend, and the text says so. After the griddle bread is made, “Crumble it and pour oil on it; it is a grain offering.” (Leviticus 2:6) It started as unleavened bread made of fine flour mixed with oil (Leviticus 2:5). So the crumbling is part of it.

Leaven is one of the two, baker. The verse says, “…you are not to burn any leaven or honey as a food offering to the LORD.” (Leviticus 2:11) That's why the oven versions are unleavened cakes and unleavened wafers (Leviticus 2:4). Bakers love a good rise, but leaven sits this one out.

Honey is the other one. The verse says, “…you are not to burn any leaven or honey as a food offering to the LORD.” (Leviticus 2:11) Even a guy who stamps cookies all day has to respect that one. Verse 12 adds that they must not go up on the altar as a pleasing aroma.

Salt is the opposite, friend. The text says, “you are to add salt to each of your offerings.” (Leviticus 2:13) It's required, so it isn't on the banned list. The two that aren't burned are leaven and honey (Leviticus 2:11).

Oil is required, not banned. The grain offering gets olive oil poured on the fine flour (Leviticus 2:1). It's mixed in or coated on, depending on how it's made (Leviticus 2:4-7). The banned two are leaven and honey (Leviticus 2:11).

Frankincense goes on the offering, friend. The text says to put it on the flour (Leviticus 2:1), and the priest burns the handful “…together with all the frankincense…” (Leviticus 2:2) So it's welcome at the altar. The two that aren't burned are leaven and honey (Leviticus 2:11).

True, baker! The text says, “You may bring them to the LORD as an offering of firstfruits, but they must not go up on the altar as a pleasing aroma.” (Leviticus 2:12) So leaven and honey can still come to the LORD as firstfruits. The limit is that they must not go up on the altar as a pleasing aroma. That “as long as” in the question holds up.

Careful, friend, that one's true, and it's an easy one to trip on. The verse begins, “You may bring them to the LORD as an offering of firstfruits…” (Leviticus 2:12) So leaven and honey are allowed as firstfruits. The limit comes at the end: “…they must not go up on the altar as a pleasing aroma.”

Salt is it. The text says, “And you shall season each of your grain offerings with salt.” (Leviticus 2:13) Then it adds, “you are to add salt to each of your offerings.” That's every offering, no exceptions.
Myrrh doesn't come up in this passage, friend. The text says, “And you shall season each of your grain offerings with salt.” (Leviticus 2:13) Salt is the one named. Myrrh stays on the shelf.

Cinnamon is a fine thing in my bakery, but it's not in this verse. The text says, “And you shall season each of your grain offerings with salt.” (Leviticus 2:13) Salt is the one the LORD names. It's always salt.

explanations.answer: Crushed new grain roasted on fire
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The LORD says, “If you bring a grain offering of firstfruits to the LORD, you shall offer crushed heads of new grain roasted on the fire.” (Leviticus 2:14) New grain, crushed, roasted on the fire. It's a different recipe from the flour ones.

explanations.answer: Whole barley soaked in cold water
explanations.explanation: Soaking and cold water aren't in this verse, friend. The text says, “…you shall offer crushed heads of new grain roasted on the fire.” (Leviticus 2:14) The grain is crushed, not whole, and it's roasted on the fire. So this one is a hot-from-the-flames kind of offering.

Wine doesn't show up in this offering. The verse says, “…you shall offer crushed heads of new grain roasted on the fire.” (Leviticus 2:14) It's grain, crushed and roasted, not flour stirred into a drink. Oil and frankincense are mentioned in the very next verse (Leviticus 2:15).

True, baker, and both halves hold. The firstfruits grain gets oil and frankincense (Leviticus 2:15). Then the priest burns the memorial portion of the crushed grain and the oil, together with all its frankincense (Leviticus 2:16). Hold on to that pattern, because it shows up again in this passage.

It's true, friend, and the text says both parts. The firstfruits grain gets oil and frankincense: “And you are to put oil and frankincense on it; it is a grain offering.” (Leviticus 2:15) The priest then burns the memorial portion of the crushed grain and the oil, together with all its frankincense (Leviticus 2:16).

explanations.answer: A male or female without blemish
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The text says, “If one’s offering is a peace offering and he offers an animal from the herd, whether male or female, he must present it without blemish before the LORD.” (Leviticus 3:1) So either one works. The animal has to be without blemish.

That was the rule for the burnt offering from the herd (Leviticus 1:3), so I see the mix-up. For the peace offering, the text says, “…whether male or female…” (Leviticus 3:1) So females are allowed this time. The no-blemish part stays.

Almost, friend, but there's still a condition. The text says it's “…whether male or female…” and “…he must present it without blemish before the LORD.” (Leviticus 3:1) So it can't have a blemish. The herd is the source, but the animal has to meet that standard.

True, baker. For the peace offering, the man lays his hand on its head and slaughters it at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting (Leviticus 3:2). The burnt offering started the same way, with a hand on the head (Leviticus 1:4). After that, Aaron's sons the priests splatter the blood on all sides of the altar.

It's true, friend. The text says, “He is to lay his hand on the head of the offering and slaughter it at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.” (Leviticus 3:2) That matches the burnt offering (Leviticus 1:4). Aaron's sons the priests are the ones who splatter the blood on all sides of the altar.

explanations.answer: The fat and kidneys and liver lobe
explanations.explanation: You got it. The text lists “the fat that covers the entrails, all the fat that is on them, both kidneys with the fat on them near the loins, and the lobe of the liver…” (Leviticus 3:3-4) That's the food offering from the peace offering. Aaron's sons then burn it on the altar atop the burnt offering (Leviticus 3:5).

explanations.answer: The head and legs and hide
explanations.explanation: The head and legs belong to the burnt offering story (Leviticus 1:8-9), not this list. For the peace offering, the text lists “the fat that covers the entrails…” “…both kidneys with the fat on them…” and “…the lobe of the liver…” (Leviticus 3:3-4) The hide isn't on this list. The peace offering has its own parts.

explanations.answer: The whole animal and its skin
explanations.explanation: Not for this offering, friend. Even the burnt offering gets skinned before it's burned (Leviticus 1:6). The peace offering's food offering is the fat, the kidneys and the lobe of the liver (Leviticus 3:3-4). Those are the parts that go up on the altar.

That's the extra. For a lamb, the list includes “the entire fat tail cut off close to the backbone…” (Leviticus 3:9) It comes right before the fat that covers the entrails. Only the lamb has the tail on the list.

The neck doesn't show up in the list, friend. The extra for a lamb is “the entire fat tail cut off close to the backbone…” (Leviticus 3:9) After that, the list goes on like the others. So it's the tail.

The shoulder isn't named here. The extra piece for a lamb is “the entire fat tail cut off close to the backbone…” (Leviticus 3:9) That's the one the verse adds. The rest of the list matches the others.

Fat is right. The text says, “Then the priest is to burn the food on the altar as a food offering, a pleasing aroma. All the fat is the LORD’s.” (Leviticus 3:16) Every time the list came up, fat was the first item. Now the LORD says all of it is His.

I can see why you'd guess meat, friend, but the text says “All the fat is the LORD’s.” (Leviticus 3:16) The list that went up on the altar was the fat, kidneys and liver lobe (Leviticus 3:14-15). So the word is fat.

Grain is the offering from the chapter before this one, friend. Here the text is on the peace offering, and it says, “All the fat is the LORD’s.” (Leviticus 3:16) The parts that went up on the altar were the fat, kidneys and liver lobe (Leviticus 3:14-15). So the word is fat.
Fat is one of the two. The LORD says, “You must not eat any fat or any blood.” (Leviticus 3:17) It's the same fat the LORD said belongs to Him in verse 16. So no fat on the menu.

Blood is the other one. The verse ends, “You must not eat any fat or any blood.” (Leviticus 3:17) Throughout the chapter, the priests splatter the blood on the altar. The people are told not to eat it.

Leaven has its own rule in chapter 2, friend. There the LORD says it can't be burned as a food offering (Leviticus 2:11). But the rule in verse 17 is “You must not eat any fat or any blood.” So leaven isn't the answer here.

Honey has its own rule in chapter 2, not this one. The LORD says honey can't be burned as a food offering (Leviticus 2:11). The rule in Leviticus 3:17 is “You must not eat any fat or any blood.” So it's not honey.

Salt is the opposite, friend. The LORD says, “you are to add salt to each of your offerings.” (Leviticus 2:13) It's required for grain offerings. The two that can't be eaten are fat and blood (Leviticus 3:17).

The text says something different, friend. It calls this “…a permanent statute for the generations to come, wherever you live…” (Leviticus 3:17) That isn't limited to the tabernacle camp. It goes on and on, wherever they live.

That's right. The LORD says, “This is a permanent statute for the generations to come, wherever you live: You must not eat any fat or any blood.” (Leviticus 3:17) It's permanent, for the generations to come, and it applies wherever they live. So it doesn't stop at the tabernacle.
